title: Building a Tree from One Grammar Rule
concept_layer: Lindenmayer systems: formal grammar as growth algorithm; string rewriting; turtle interpretation; bracketed branching

capture_leaks.deterministic_growth: F → F[+F]F[-F]F runs the same way every time. Real plants have randomness, environmental response, gene expression variance. Stochastic L-systems (next map) introduce randomness; ecological L-systems introduce context.
capture_leaks.string_alphabet_small: We use F, +, -, [, ], but L-systems can have arbitrary alphabets. Parametric L-systems attach values to symbols (F(length), +(angle)).
capture_leaks.no_death: Branches don’t wither. Real plants prune, shed, heal. L-systems handle this with special symbols, but this artifact doesn’t.
capture_leaks.no_environment: The grammar runs in vacuum — no light, no gravity response (phototropism), no collision. LSystems_Living adds environmental feedback.
capture_leaks.bracketed_trees_only: The [ ] convention makes the structure a tree. Graphs, cycles, mergers are awkward. Graph grammars (graphtheory sequence) handle those.

limit: One axiom. One rule. One angle. A plant. The artifact demonstrates that grammar — a formal system of symbol-replacement — is enough to generate organic-looking form. What it refuses: stochastic variation, contextual rules, parametric symbols, environmental response, death. Each of those is a door that later L-systems maps open. This is the seed of the entire sequence.

grammar_alignment.note: lsystem_tree teaches THREE operations simultaneously — it is the densest grammar artifact. rewrite expands the string, turtle_interpret converts symbols to geometry, branch pushes/pops state via [ ]. Each is a separate concept but they compose so tightly that teaching them together is cleaner than apart.

biome_alignment.note: CRITICAL BIOME TRANSITION. First appearance of the 'creature' kingdom — the world now has animals. Movement gets 'climb' — the player can reach elevated terrain by climbing plants. 'write_rule' and 'branch_grow' verbs let the player literally author a grammar and watch it grow. This is the sequence where the world becomes ALIVE.

stages.title: From recursion to grammar
stages.thinking: Fractal_Recursion taught that a function that calls itself with smaller parameters produces self-similar form. Now a different language for the same kind of thing. Instead of a function, a STRING. Instead of function calls, STRING REWRITES. Start with 'F' (the axiom). Replace every 'F' with 'F[+F]F[-F]F' (the rule). Repeat. The string grows. Then interpret each symbol as a drawing instruction and you have a tree. Grammar is recursion written as text.
stages.code:
# Fractal_Recursion:
#   function generate_branch(depth):
#     if depth > 0:
#       generate_branch(depth - 1)  # self-call
#       generate_branch(depth - 1)  # another self-call
#
# L-system:
#   axiom: "F"
#   rule:  F → F[+F]F[-F]F
#
#   iteration 0: F
#   iteration 1: F[+F]F[-F]F
#   iteration 2: F[+F]F[-F]F[+F[+F]F[-F]F]F[+F]F[-F]F[-F[+F]F[-F]F]F[+F]F[-F]F
#   iteration 4: ~1200 characters, looks like a plant
#
# Same computation, different representation.

stages.title: The classic Lindenmayer rule
stages.thinking: F → F[+F]F[-F]F. Six symbols. F means 'step forward.' + means 'turn left.' - means 'turn right.' [ means 'save state.' ] means 'restore state.' Starting with just F, after 4 iterations, you have a string that, when interpreted, draws a realistic plant. This specific rule is Lindenmayer’s original. Changing it subtly (F → FF[+F]F[-F] or F[+F][-F]F) gives a different species. Grammar IS species.

stages.title: Rewrite the string N times
stages.thinking: For each iteration, walk through the current string and replace every F with its expansion. Other symbols (+, -, [, ]) are copied as-is. After N iterations, the string has grown exponentially. At iteration 4 with this rule, the string is about 1,200 characters. At iteration 6, it’s over 100,000. This is why iteration count is bounded — memory and render cost explode.
stages.code:
func _derive_string() -> String:
	var current := AXIOM
	for i in range(iterations):
		var next := ""
		for c in current:
			if RULES.has(c):
				next += RULES[c]
			else:
				next += c  # non-F symbols pass through
		current = next
	return current

# String lengths for rule F → F[+F]F[-F]F:
#   iter 0:    1 char (just 'F')
#   iter 1:    9 chars
#   iter 2:   81 chars
#   iter 3:  729 chars
#   iter 4: 6561 chars (default max)
#   iter 5:  59k chars (too many lines for VR)

stages.title: The turtle — interpret symbols as drawing commands
stages.thinking: A 'turtle' is a virtual pen with position and heading. F: move forward, drawing a segment. +: turn left by base_angle. -: turn right. After deriving the string, walk it symbol by symbol, driving the turtle. Result: a geometric form. The turtle is the simplest interface between symbolic computation and visual form. Seymour Papert’s invention; LOGO’s heart; the missing link between text and picture.
stages.code:
var turtle_pos: Vector3
var turtle_heading: Vector3  # unit vector
var turtle_up: Vector3       # for 3D turning
var turtle_stack: Array = []  # for [ ] bracketing

func _interpret(s: String) -> void:
	turtle_pos = Vector3.ZERO
	turtle_heading = Vector3.UP
	turtle_up = Vector3.BACK
	turtle_stack.clear()
	
	var lines = []
	for c in s:
		match c:
			"F":
				var new_pos = turtle_pos + turtle_heading * base_length
				lines.append([turtle_pos, new_pos])
				turtle_pos = new_pos
			"+":
				turtle_heading = turtle_heading.rotated(turtle_up, deg_to_rad(base_angle))
			"-":
				turtle_heading = turtle_heading.rotated(turtle_up, -deg_to_rad(base_angle))
			"[":
				turtle_stack.push_back([turtle_pos, turtle_heading, turtle_up])
			"]":
				var state = turtle_stack.pop_back()
				turtle_pos = state[0]
				turtle_heading = state[1]
				turtle_up = state[2]
	return lines

stages.title: The square brackets — save and restore state
stages.thinking: [ pushes turtle state onto a stack. ] pops it, restoring position and heading. Between a matching [ and ], the turtle wanders — then snaps back as if nothing happened. This is branching. Without [ ], a string like F[+F]F would make the turtle turn, draw, turn back, draw more — not a branch but a zigzag. The stack gives us recursion in-place without function calls.
stages.code:
# [ ] is the hinge between strings and trees.
#
# Without stack:
#   F+F-F    draws a zigzag (one line)
#
# With stack:
#   F[+F][-F]F    draws a trunk with two branches
#        ^^^^ 'save state' before turning,
#              draw branch,
#              'restore' and continue
#
# The stack makes a flat string represent a tree.
# LIFO push/pop IS hierarchy.

"[":
	turtle_stack.push_back([turtle_pos, turtle_heading, turtle_up])
"]":
	var state = turtle_stack.pop_back()
	turtle_pos = state[0]
	turtle_heading = state[1]
	turtle_up = state[2]

stages.title: Render the line segments with depth coloring
stages.thinking: After the turtle walks the string, we have a list of (start, end) line segments. Render them with ImmediateMesh. The trick: color based on how deep the segment is in the tree (how many [ ] above it). Trunk = brown. Deep branches = green. This gives the tree its plant-like appearance without any extra code — the structure itself produces the gradient.

stages.title: Parameters — iteration count, angle, base length
stages.thinking: Three @export sliders. Iterations (1-5): sapling to forest giant. Base angle (10-45 degrees): palm (wide) to pine (narrow) to bush (spread). Base length (0.05-0.2): compact to sprawling. Same axiom, same rule — three parameters turn the grammar into a species. This is the real lesson: L-systems are not 'one plant' but a parameterized family. Change two numbers and get a different genus.

stages.title: Give it identity
stages.thinking: The L-system tree knows what it is. Not a plant — a DEMONSTRATION that grammar is growth. One rule, one axiom, one angle. Repeat four times, interpret, render. The whole sequence follows from this atom: stochastic variants, context-sensitive rules, parametric attributes, ecological feedback. But all of them begin with F → F[+F]F[-F]F. The tree is the proof that Lindenmayer found in 1968: plants are computable, and the computation is short.
